Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Question 1(a) : « Briefly explain the origin of the universe » : le corrigé donne la théorie du Big Bang (âge d'environ 13,8 milliards d'années, valeur de cours) et ses trois preuves classiques ; les théories concurrentes (état stationnaire, univers oscillant) ne sont que citées.

Question 1(b) : profondeurs et vitesses des ondes P aux discontinuités données comme ordres de grandeur de cours (formulation « about »). La discontinuité de Conrad n'est pas détectée partout et sa définition varie un peu selon les manuels (limite croûte supérieure granitique / croûte inférieure basaltique retenue).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Briefly explain the origin of the universe.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The Big Bang theory** is the accepted explanation of the origin of the universe.

1. **Beginning.** About **13.8 billion years ago** all matter and energy were concentrated in an extremely hot, dense point (a singularity). It **expanded suddenly and very rapidly** (the "Big Bang"), and space itself has been expanding ever since.
2. **Cooling and first matter.** As the universe expanded it **cooled**. Within the first minutes, protons and neutrons combined to form the nuclei of the lightest elements: **hydrogen (about 75 per cent by mass), helium (about 25 per cent)** and traces of lithium. After about 380 000 years the temperature was low enough for atoms to form and light could travel freely.
3. **Stars and galaxies.** **Gravity** pulled the gas clouds together into denser regions. These collapsed to form the **first stars and galaxies** (a few hundred million years after the Big Bang). Heavier elements were made inside stars and scattered by supernova explosions, and later clouds of this material formed new stars, planets and our **solar system** (about 4.6 billion years ago).

**Evidence for the theory:** (i) the **red shift** of light from distant galaxies, which shows that galaxies are moving away from one another (Hubble's law); (ii) the **cosmic microwave background radiation** (about 2.7 K), the cooled remains of the early hot universe; (iii) the observed **abundance of hydrogen and helium**, which agrees with the predictions of the theory. (Rival ideas, such as the steady-state and the oscillating-universe theories, are not supported by this evidence.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Give the significance of each of the following discontinuities:

(i) Conrad discontinuity;

(3 marks)

(ii) Moho discontinuity;

(3 marks)

(iii) Gutenberg discontinuity.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **seismic discontinuity** is a boundary inside the Earth across which the **velocity of seismic waves changes suddenly**, because the rock changes in composition, density or physical state. Discontinuities are the main evidence for the layered structure of the Earth.

**(i) Conrad discontinuity.** It separates the **upper continental crust (sial: granitic, less dense)** from the **lower continental crust (sima: basaltic or gabbroic, denser)**, at a depth of about 15 to 20 km (it varies and is not found everywhere). Across it the velocity of P-waves rises slightly, from about 6.0 to about 6.6 km/s. It shows that the continental crust is **not uniform** but has two layers. It is absent under the oceans, where the crust is thin and basaltic.

**(ii) Moho (Mohorovicic) discontinuity.** It is the boundary between the **crust and the mantle**, found by the Croatian seismologist Mohorovicic in 1909. It lies at about **5 to 10 km under the oceans**, about **30 to 40 km under the continents** and up to about 70 km under young fold mountains. Across it the velocity of P-waves jumps sharply, from about 6.5 to 7 km/s in the lower crust to about **8 km/s** in the peridotitic upper mantle, because the mantle rock is denser. It defines the **base of the crust** and shows the change from crustal (granite, basalt) to ultrabasic mantle rock; seismic waves are also partly reflected and refracted there.

**(iii) Gutenberg discontinuity.** It is the boundary between the **mantle and the outer core**, at a depth of about **2 900 km**, found by Beno Gutenberg in 1914. Across it the velocity of P-waves **falls suddenly** (from about 13.7 km/s to about 8 km/s) and **S-waves stop completely**. This shows that the **outer core is liquid** (molten iron and nickel), since S-waves cannot pass through a liquid, and it causes the **shadow zones** of earthquake waves on the opposite side of the Earth. It also shows the large change in density and composition between the silicate mantle and the metallic core.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Differentiate between the following pairs:

(i) Earthquake focus and earthquake epicentre;

(2 marks)

(ii) Body wave and surface wave;

(2 marks)

(iii) Seismograph and seismogram.

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Focus and epicentre.** The **focus (hypocentre)** is the **point inside the Earth** where the rocks break and the earthquake starts, from which the seismic waves spread out in all directions. The **epicentre** is the **point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus**, where the shaking is usually strongest. The focus is underground (at a depth of a few km to about 700 km), the epicentre is on the surface.

**(ii) Body wave and surface wave.** **Body waves (P-waves and S-waves)** travel **through the interior** of the Earth, are **faster**, have smaller amplitude and arrive first (P-waves, then S-waves). **Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh waves)** travel **only along the Earth's surface**, starting from the epicentre, are **slower**, arrive last, have large amplitude and long wavelength and cause **most of the damage**.

**(iii) Seismograph and seismogram.** A **seismograph** is the **instrument** that detects and records ground vibrations (a heavy mass that stays almost still while the frame moves with the ground, connected to a recording system). A **seismogram** is the **record (trace or graph of ground motion against time)** that the seismograph produces, from which the arrival times of the P, S and surface waves and the magnitude and distance of the earthquake are read.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) What do you understand by the following geological concepts?

(i) Sea-floor spreading;

(3 marks)

(ii) Plate tectonics.

(3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sea-floor spreading.** It is the process (proposed by Harry Hess in the early 1960s) by which **new oceanic crust is formed at the mid-oceanic ridges** and **moves away on both sides** of the ridge. **Magma rises** from the mantle into the gap that opens along the ridge axis (divergent boundary), cools and solidifies as **basalt and gabbro**, and is then split and carried sideways by newer magma. The ocean floor therefore gets **older, cooler and covered by thicker sediment away from the ridge**, and is destroyed again by **subduction in the trenches**. Evidence: **symmetrical magnetic stripes** (normal and reversed polarity) on both sides of the ridge, the **age of the ocean-floor rocks increasing away from the ridge**, thin sediments at the ridge, and high heat flow at the ridge.

**(ii) Plate tectonics.** It is the theory that the **lithosphere (crust and uppermost rigid mantle) is broken into a small number of large rigid plates** (seven major ones and several minor ones) that **move slowly (a few cm per year)** over the weaker, partly molten **asthenosphere**, carried mainly by **mantle convection**, ridge push and slab pull. The plates **interact at their boundaries**: **divergent** (plates move apart, new crust forms), **convergent** (plates collide, one is subducted or mountains are formed) and **transform** (plates slide past each other). Most **earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building and ocean trenches** occur along these boundaries. The theory unites continental drift and sea-floor spreading.
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading
